title: Fire Ranging on Grass
subtitle: The Sarnga bow answers the Asura host at Shatpura.
story:
When Krishna set string to the Sarnga bow, the Asuras saw their death approaching, and being Asuras, they charged straight into it.

Anadhrishti and the other captains had been swallowed by the cave of Shatpura, taken one by one through Nikumbha's illusion. The Yadava army still stood, but its heart was inside the mountain. There was only one answer left, and Krishna gave it. He drew the Sarnga and began to move among the Danavas.

He moved as fire ranges over dry grass: not running, not pausing, simply advancing, and everything ahead of him burned. The comparison was no ornament. Fire does not fight the grass; it passes through it, and the grass is gone. The Sarnga's arrows flew before him in sheets, and wherever he stepped, the Danava host found itself standing in the path of a blaze.

The Danavas did not understand what they were seeing. To them he was one man with a bow, and they had a mountain's worth of weapons. They took up thousands of sataghnis and parighas, fiery lances and burning axes; they tore up dreadful rocks and great stones; they hurled infuriated elephants, chariots and horses; and they ran at him with all of it, like locusts driven by the noose of Death into a burning fire. The whole arsenal of the mountain came down on Krishna in one tremendous shower.

The Narayana-fire consumed it all. The flung weapons, the stones, the maddened elephants, the chariots, all of it met the blaze of his arrows and was gone. And Krishna, smiling, baffled them all, standing under the downpour as a bull stands in autumn rain, patient and unhurried and untouched. He had been smiling since he strung the bow, and the smile, in the end, was more terrible than the fire.

Then the host tried to run. Some broke for the sky, rising on whatever dark power they had left, seeking the one direction an army believes is safe: upward, into the open air.

It was not safe. The sky was not empty. Above the field, hidden where only Krishna could see them, waited Jayanta and Pravara, called up by a thought before the battle began. As soon as any Asura rose into the sky, their arrows met him, and every one of them fell. The Asuras who remained looked up and understood, too late, that the one direction they had left unguarded was guarded. The sky became a wall.

And so the Danava host was caught between two deaths: the fire ranging on the ground, and the silent archers who owned the air. The Danava host was not beaten yet, it was burning: the numbers they had trusted, the weapons they had trusted, the fury they had trusted, all of it ash in the path of one smiling archer. The plain filled with the wreck of their courage. Their roar died into the dust, and the rout that Nikumbha's illusion had postponed came at last, in full.

Krishna lowered the Sarnga bow. The fire had done its ranging, and the grass was gone. Beyond the smoke stood the cave of Shatpura, still holding its prisoners.

The battle was won. The cave was not.
reflection: The rout has the shape of a parable about fear: the host that charges a burning fire, and the few who escape, are met by the one force they forgot, the sky, where Jayanta and Pravara have waited unseen all along. Krishna's calm throughout, smiling and bearing the shower like a bull in rain, is the story's true wonder.
